latin: Ursus abbas<sup>1</sup> monasterium statuit, situm scilicet<sup>2</sup> apud flumen Angerem<sup>3</sup>...
in recessu<sup>4</sup> montis cui nunc castrum<sup>5</sup> imminet, eodem nomine quo monasterium appellatum.
Cum fratres molam manu vertentes, triticum<sup>6</sup> ad victum<sup>7</sup> necessarium comminuerent<sup>8</sup>...
pro<sup>9</sup> labore fratrum visum est ei molendinum<sup>10</sup> in ipso Angeris fluvii alveo<sup>11</sup>, instituere.
Defixis<sup>12</sup> in flumine sublicis, congregatis lapidum magnorum acervis<sup>13</sup>, claustra<sup>14</sup> fecit...
atque aquam canali<sup>15</sup> collegit<sup>16</sup>, cujus impetu fabricae<sup>17</sup> rota magna volubilitate circumacta est<sup>18</sup>.
Hoc opere laborem monachorum relevavit, atque id uni<sup>19</sup> fratrum delegavit.
Quae sententiae e Vitis Patrum excerptae sunt, qui liber a Gregorio Turonensi scriptus est.
english: Abbot Ursus had established a monastery, [situated] (namely) on the bank of the river Indre...
in a fold of a hill [which] (to which) a castle called by the same name (abl.) as the monastery now dominates.
While the brothers, [turning] the millstone by hand, were grinding (subj.) the wheat necessary for their subsistence...
[to replace the] (in the place of) work of the brothers, he had the idea (it seemed to him) of setting up a mill in the very bed of the river Indre.
Stakes having been driven into the river, [and] piles of large stones having been gathered, he made a dam...
and collected the water in a canal, by the force of which the wheel of a machine was driven at great speed.
[Thanks] to this work, he relieved [the monks of their] (the work of the monks), and entrusted this (charge) to a single one of the brothers.
Thus the necessary work was done.
These sentences have been extracted from the Life of the Fathers, which book was written by Gregory of Tours.

footnotes: Abbas, -atis, m., the abbot (superior of a monastery).
Scilicet = scire licet, it is permitted to know, namely.
Anger, -eris, m., the Indre (river). Fluvius, -i, m., or flumen, -inis, n.: have the same meaning and mean river as well as stream.

Castrum is a rarity, for this word is only used in the plural: castra, -orum, pl. n., the camp. Its diminutive castellum, -i, n., means a fairly small fortified work, a fortified castle. Cui, dative of the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod, governed by the verb imminet (imminere, to be suspended above: we have already seen eminere, L. 54, N. 2).
Triticum, -i, n., wheat; frumentum, -i, n., grain, is more common.
Victus, -us, m., derived from vivere, to live.
Minuo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to diminish (cf. minute), whence comminuere, comminuerent (3rd pers. pl. subj. impf.).
Pro + abl., in front, in place of..., it would be more correct to use the adj. verbal of an appropriate verb, e.g.: ad laborem fratrum levandum, to relieve (levare) the work of the brothers.
Molendinum, -i, n., mill. In classical Latin, one would rather say mola, -ae, the millstone, or in the pl. molae, -arum, the mill (cf. the title of the lesson).
Alveus, -i, m., hollow, location of the bed of a river (cf. alveolus).

Defigo, -is, -ere, fixi, fixum: not to be confused with figere, to plant, to fix, and fingere, finxi, fictum, to fashion, to invent. Sublica, -ae, f., stake, pile. Sublicis defixis: ablative absolute; likewise, further down, congregatis acervis.
Acervus, -i, m., heap; coacervare, to amass, to pile up; congregare, to gather (from grex, gregis, m.).
Claustrum, -i, n., closure, dam (cf. French cloître, cloister); comes from claudere, to close.

Fabrica, -ae, f., rather designates the forge, the factory or manufacture; here machine, in the sense of manufactured object. Volvo, -is, -ere, volvi, volutum, to roll, to turn (around an axis); derivatives: volubilitas, aptitude to turn, and figuratively: suppleness, fluency of language; volumen, -inis, n., book, for formerly books were ROLLS of papyrus or parchment.
Circumagere, to push around, to make turn. Here in the perfect passive.
Uni, dative singular of unus (see R. and N. no. 49).
comments: You will find a more complete extract of this story, closer to the original text, in Textes latins du Moyen Age, by Jean Delannoy (Editions O.C.D.L., Paris).

This lesson, whose original text we have already considerably modified so as not to trouble your mind, gives you an example of late Latin that is not very classical and should not be taken as a model. We have nevertheless wanted to give you, in this lesson as in the next, examples of low Latin, so as not to call it kitchen Latin. Simply remember that these good people were not expecting to be Cicero's rivals when they wrote in Latin. So do not hesitate to do as they did. Nothing will prevent you afterwards from perfecting yourself by reading good authors and by having your letters corrected by expert friends.

You can even perfect yourself in an amusing way by noting a few faults of low Latin: for example, the use of improper or needlessly complicated words, or the abuse of prefixes or suffixes. Moreover today too many people, forgetting the resources of their mother tongue, do not hesitate to use words such as «solutionner» where «résoudre» would be quite enough.

Tero, -is, -ere, trivi, tritum, to grind, to crush; figuratively note trita via, a beaten path. — Haurire, to draw (4th decl., pft hausi, supine haustum); exhaurire, to exhaust; to pump would be more precisely: antlare and likewise exantlare, to empty completely with a pump, whence to exhaust (in the literal and figurative sense). We have already seen antlia (L. 40, P. 9). Antlia Pneumatica, the Pneumatic Machine, is also a constellation of the southern hemisphere. — Palus, -udis, f., the marsh (think of paludism); its homonym palus, -i, m., stake, post, has a less precise meaning than sublica, which we permitted ourselves to substitute for it in sentence 5 of the lesson. — Obsolesco, -is, -ere, -levi, -letum, to go out of fashion (cf. the English adjective obsolete).

latin: Triticum seu frumentum mola teritur, id est in farinam redigitur.
Molae antiquae vi hominum vel animalium agebantur.
Medio aevo, molae vi fluminum actae jam divulgatae erant.
In Batavia autem vis venti, quae machinarum haud dissimilium alas movet, non solum ad triticum molendum, sed etiam ad aquam rivorum paludumque exhauriendam, usurpabatur.
Nunc haec omnia obsoleverunt et in imaginibus tantum videntur.
Molae enim hodiernae vi electrica aguntur.
english: Wheat or corn is crushed by the millstone, that is [to say] it is reduced to flour.
The ancient millstones were set in motion by the force of men or [of] animals.
In the Middle Ages, [water mills] (mills set in motion by the force of rivers) were already widespread.
But in Holland, the force of the wind, which pushes the sails of fairly similar machines, was used not only to grind wheat, but also to [pump] (exhaust) the water of streams and marshes.
Now all these things are obsolete and can only be seen in pictures.
In fact modern mills [run on] (are set in motion by) electric force.
